description:
Code 404 is a solo team: a multimedia designer working in website design, UI/UX and digital marketing. Our project, ECHO’s Lost Memories, teaches kids aged 7–10 about the 14 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars through mini-games and short stories based on real missions.

This challenge needed design as much as research. My background let me build the whole thing myself: the story, characters, interface and games, designed for small hands and early readers.
summary:
ECHO’s Lost Memories is an interactive web story that introduces kids aged 7 to 10 to the 14 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, from Surveyor 3 and Apollo 11’s Eagle to Opportunity and Ingenuity.

Players meet ECHO, a little archive robot whose memories of these machines were scrambled by a solar storm. To help ECHO remember, kids follow blinking beacons to real landing sites, play a short mini-game based on how each mission actually worked (such as landing Eagle or finding Opportunity’s “blueberries”), and unlock that machine’s story. Each machine tells it in its own voice: the problem it faced, the clever engineering, what it discovered, and where it is now.

The goal was to replace dense facts with a story kids feel part of. Every memory connects hardware to science. For example, Opportunity’s rock grinder led to the discovery that liquid water once soaked Mars. Facts come from NASA’s public records. Read-aloud narration, quizzes, mission patches and a timeline keep the experience accessible and rewarding. It runs in any browser on a phone, tablet or computer.
details:
ECHO’s Lost Memories is an interactive, story-driven website that teaches kids aged 7 to 10 about the 14 machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, and the science they made possible.

The player meets ECHO, a little archive robot that once kept the memories of every machine humans left on other worlds. A solar storm scrambled those memories and scattered them back to where the machines were left. The player becomes the explorer who helps ECHO remember, because “every machine has a last message, and if nobody hears it, it’s really gone.”

How does it work?

  1. Wake ECHO up. A short intro (restore ECHO’s power, name your explorer) and a comic-strip prologue set up the mission.
  2. Follow the beacons. A space map leads to a zoomable map of the Moon’s near side (Act I, “Together”, 1967–1972) and a flat map of Mars (Act II, “Alone”, 1976 onward). Each blinking beacon sits at a real landing site.
  3. Play the mission. Each memory is “scrambled” behind a mini-game based on how that mission actually worked. Kids land Apollo 11’s Eagle past the boulders, fire Surveyor 3’s braking engines to touch down softly, rebuild the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover, and find Opportunity’s “blueberries” among the Martian pebbles. Games can be skipped, so no child gets stuck.
  4. The machine tells its story. Each memory unfolds in four comic panels, told by the machine in its own personality: the problem, the clever part (the engineering), the discovery (the science), and where it is now. Supporting cards cover “What we learned”, a size check, “The people behind it”, “Space nerd mode” with mission data, and links between related memories.
  5. Learn, listen, collect. A one-question quiz checks understanding. “Read it to me” reads each story aloud. Kids earn stars, ranks, mission patches and achievements, and can put the machines in order on a timeline.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns dense historical and technical records into short, playful stories that a 7-year-old can follow.
  • Kids learn by doing (landing, steering, searching), not by memorising lists.
  • It covers both worlds and over five decades of exploration: crewed Apollo hardware and robotic Mars explorers.
  • It’s free, works in any browser, and needs no account.

What is the intended impact?
School-age kids mostly hear about current missions. We want them to know the machines that came first, understand why each was sent and what it taught us, and feel a personal connection to these “forgotten” explorers. We hope that curiosity grows into an interest in science and engineering. Teachers and parents can also use it as a ready-made, accurate classroom or at-home activity.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in a single-page web app, with no frameworks.
  • SVG for all illustrations: ECHO, the machines and the Moon and Mars maps.
  • The HTML Canvas for the mini-games.
  • The Web Audio API for sound effects and the Web Speech API for “Read it to me” narration.
  • Netlify for hosting.

Data sources: NASA’s public records, including the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) Master Catalog and NASA Science, plus real Apollo 11 mission audio.

How is your project creative?

  • A narrator with a stake in the story. ECHO isn’t a guide reciting facts. It has lost something, and the child is the one who can fix it. Each recovered memory fills ECHO’s memory bar, from 0 to 14.
  • The machines speak. Each has its own voice and personality, such as Eagle the “calm guardian” and Opportunity the “cheerful marathon runner”, so kids remember them as characters.
  • Games that teach the mission. Each mini-game is the mission’s real challenge, simplified. For example, kids land Eagle because Neil Armstrong really had to fly past a boulder field.
  • A two-act structure. “Together” on the Moon, where humans and robots explored side by side, and “Alone” on Mars, where the robots went without us.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Age group (7–10): short sentences, comic panels, big tap targets, friendly characters, and skippable games so no child gets stuck.
  • Accuracy: every fact is drawn from NASA’s public records. ECHO and the machines’ voices are clearly labelled as invented for the story.
  • Accessibility: read-aloud narration for early and struggling readers. Mouse, touch and keyboard controls. Labels for screen readers. A reduced-motion setting is respected. It works on phones, tablets and computers.
  • Privacy and safety: no sign-up and no personal data collected. The explorer name and progress stay on the child’s own device.
  • Engagement: stars, ranks, patches and achievements reward finishing the stories, quizzes and games.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

  • Building the interactive website. Claude helped generate and debug the HTML, CSS and JavaScript for our site’s layout, interactive parts and data visualizations. We designed the site, decided what it should do and how users move through it, and then reviewed, tested and changed the AI-suggested code before using it.
  • Coding. Claude helped write and fix code for loading, cleaning and processing the data. Our team checked every piece of AI-assisted code by running it against the real datasets and confirming the outputs were correct. AI-assisted files are noted in the repository README under “AI Use.”
  • Reading and understanding data resources. Claude helped us read the NASA and Space Agency Partner documentation, dataset descriptions and file formats, and summarize them, so we could understand them faster. We chose which datasets to use and made our own interpretation of the data and the conclusions we drew from it. We checked these against the original sources.
  • Fact-checking support: Claude cross-checked facts in the scripts and descriptions against the text on our website, which is sourced from NASA’s public records (the NSSDCA Master Catalog and NASA Science
